quote: Als 24stes Problem in meinem Pariser Vortrag wollte ich die Frage stellen: Kriterien für die Einfach- heit bez. Beweis der grössten Einfachheit von [-?-] gewissen Beweisen führen.
english: As the 24th problem in my Paris lecture I wanted to pose the question: criteria for the simplicity of certain proofs, or proof of the greatest simplicity of certain proofs.
topic: Hilbert notes a plan to analyse linkage constructions for the simplest apparatus, then describes the problem he had wanted to pose as the 24th problem of his Paris lecture: criteria for the simplicity of proofs and a theory of proof methods, with syzygies as an example.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert's '24th problem' (unpublished): find criteria, ideally formal ones, for how simple a mathematical proof is, and build a theory of proof methods strong enough to show that a given proof is the simplest one for a theorem under given conditions. Hilbert's example was proofs about syzygies. In modern terms the question sits between proof theory (normalization, identity of proofs, proof complexity and proof length) and automated reasoning (finding the shortest or simplest proofs). 'Simplicity' has no single agreed formal definition, so the question is a programme rather than one well-posed theorem.
triage.answered_by: Not solved. Hilbert dropped it from the 1900 Paris lecture and never published it. The historian Rüdiger Thiele found it in Hilbert's notebooks in 2000 and published it as 'Hilbert's Twenty-Fourth Problem' (American Mathematical Monthly 110(1), 2003, pp. 1-24). Later partial work includes Larry Wos (automated reasoning, shortest proofs, with Thiele) and the Royal Society Phil. Trans. A theme issue 'Hilbert's 24th problem' (vol. 377, 2019).

evidence.claim: The 24th problem was not among the 23 published problems. It was in Hilbert's notes and asks for a criterion of simplicity for proofs, plus a proof theory able to show that a given proof is the simplest.

Rüdiger Thiele rediscovered it in 2000. Hilbert did not include it in the lecture or in any published text. Wikipedia's quotation of the note includes the line about judging the simplicity of proofs in his work on syzygies.
Thiele's paper 'Hilbert's Twenty-Fourth Problem' appeared in The American Mathematical Monthly, Vol. 110, No. 1 (2003), pp. 1-24.

After Thiele published the problem, various scholars took up the question of simplicity in different forms. Related topics include the logical representation of proofs, proof length, and computational complexity (e.g. the idea of a simplest algorithm).
One line of research that grew out of the problem is the identification of proofs, i.e. deciding when two proofs count as the same.
Larry Wos published on the 24th problem and its relation to automated reasoning, logic and mathematics.

triage.why: The diary passage matches the text of the note Thiele found and published as Hilbert's 24th problem: the Paris lecture, criteria of simplicity, proof of the greatest simplicity, and syzygies as the example. So this is now a well-known, named problem, though it was published long after the fact and was never one of the official 23. It has not been solved, partly because there is no agreed formal notion of 'simplicity'. Work on it continues in proof theory, identity of proofs, proof complexity and automated reasoning, including a 2019 Royal Society theme issue. The 2019 date comes from my own knowledge, not the sources I found: the page I retrieved shows volume 377 but no year.
